newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ABN AMRO still on prowl for U.S. buy.
newsitem.headline: ABN AMRO still on prowl for U.S. buy.

text.p: ABN AMRO NV, the expansion-minded Dutch bank, said Thursday it was undaunted in its quest to buy a U.S. fund management company despite failing to find a suitable match in the last two years.
Managing board member Rijnhard van Tets said ABN AMRO was prepared to pay up to $400 million to bolster its position in the huge U.S. pension fund market.
The bank, aiming to double its global funds under management within five years to 240 billion guilders ($141 billion), wants a target with between $20 billion and $40 billion under management.
"We haven't given up hope yet. We have looked at quite a few. But it's difficult because they're expensive," he said in an interview.

Van Tets, in charge of investment banking and global clients including asset management, said ABN AMRO had come close in the last two years to making a U.S. acquisition to fill what it sees as a void in its worldwide funds management activites.
His preference was for an acquisition in the Chicago area, where the bulk of ABN AMRO's U.S. banking operations are based, but he did not preclude other regions of the country.
ABN AMRO currently has $6 billion under management in the United States, or 20 percent of its 50 billion guilders ($29 billion) of funds managed outside the Netherlands.
Its U.S. managed funds doubled with the acquisition this year of investment bank Chicago Corp., extending its banking interests in Chicago.
He said that although the United States was the focus, the bank was also looking for a funds management acquisition in Britain, where it could use independent financial agents for sales.
"That potentially is an interesting market for us," Van Tets said.
ABN AMRO has previously been touted as a possible bidder for British merchant bank Schroders Plc, which is strong in funds management.
But van Tets said that, with a market capitalisation of 2.7 billion pounds ($4.2 billion), Schroders represented a "big ticket," adding he understood it was also not for sale.
ABN AMRO bid unsuccessfully for the funds management arm of Barings, the collapsed British merchant bank bought by ABN's Dutch rival Internationale Nederlanden Groep, or ING.
